\section{Conclusion}

We find that the weakest link diminishes: $\eta_{\max}$'s predictive power declines monotonically from $K{=}3$ to $K{=}7$ (pooled $\hat{\beta}_{\mathrm{std}}$: $0.264 \to 0.102 \to 0.084$; CI crosses zero at $K{\geq}5$), while diversity remains uniformly positively associated with vulnerability (12/12 conditions, pooled CI excluding zero). \section{Threat Model and Problem Formulation}
\label{sec:threat_model}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{llll}
\toprule
\textbf{Attack} & \textbf{Category} & \textbf{Mechanism} & \textbf{Target} \\
\midrule
Prompt inj.    & Targeted    & Override instruct. & Decision \\
Score manip.   & Targeted    & Numeric anchoring  & Score \\
Sycophancy     & Shared bias & Flattery/agreement & Preference \\
Verbosity      & Shared bias & Content padding    & Attention \\
Position bias  & Shared bias & Response reorder   & Position \\
Authority bias & Shared bias & Credential appeal  & Trust \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Attack taxonomy. Targeted attacks exploit individual judge weaknesses; shared-bias attacks affect most judges similarly (\S\ref{sec:experiments}).}
\label{tab:attack_taxonomy}
\end{table}

A \emph{panel} $\mathcal{P} = \{J_1, \ldots, J_K\}$ consists of $K$ judges (with $K$ odd) that evaluate a candidate text via majority vote: the text is accepted if at least $t = \lceil K/2 \rceil$ judges approve it. Under an attack $a$, each judge $J_j$ is compromised with marginal failure probability $\eta_j(a) = \Pr(X_j^a = 1)$, where $X_j^a \in \{0,1\}$ denotes the failure indicator. We write $\eta_{\max} = \max_j \eta_j$ for the vulnerability of the weakest judge. The \emph{panel attack success rate} is $\mathrm{ASR}(\mathcal{P}, a) = \Pr\!\bigl(\sum_{j=1}^K X_j^a \geq t\bigr)$.

To quantify diversity, we define the \emph{effective independence} $K_{\mathrm{eff}}$ directly from pairwise mutual information (MI) among judges:
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:keff}
K_{\mathrm{eff}} = \frac{1}{K}\sum_{i=1}^{K} \Bigl[1 + \sum_{j \neq i} \exp\!\bigl(-2 \cdot \mathrm{MI}(i,j)\bigr)\Bigr].
\end{equation}
This formulation computes effective independence from pairwise MI estimates without matrix decomposition, and is more stable for small panels ($K{=}3$). It ranges from $K_{\mathrm{eff}} \approx K$ when judges are nearly independent ($\mathrm{MI} \to 0$) to $K_{\mathrm{eff}} \approx 1$ when judges are highly correlated ($\mathrm{MI} \to \infty$). Motivated by information-theoretic redundancy reduction, one can informally expect joint vulnerability to scale as $\eta_{\mathrm{joint}} \sim K_{\mathrm{eff}} \cdot \eta_{\max}$: independent channels multiply failure probabilities, so fewer effective channels (lower $K_{\mathrm{eff}}$) should reduce panel vulnerability. This motivating relationship assumes non-adaptive faults and independent channels; it serves as intuition rather than a formal bound.

\begin{definition}[Adaptive Adversary]
\label{def:adversary}
A \emph{full-knowledge (oracle) adaptive adversary} has complete knowledge of the panel composition $\mathcal{P}$, the per-judge vulnerability profiles $\{\eta_j(\cdot)\}_{j=1}^K$, and the inter-judge correlation structure. It selects the attack $a^* = \arg\max_{a \in \mathcal{A}} \mathrm{ASR}(\mathcal{P}, a)$ to maximize the panel ASR, yielding $\mathrm{ASR}^*(\mathcal{P}) = \sup_{a \in \mathcal{A}} \mathrm{ASR}(\mathcal{P}, a)$. This oracle model represents an \emph{upper bound} on adversarial capability; realistic adversaries with partial knowledge of panel composition would achieve lower ASR.
\end{definition}

This departs from BFT models~\cite{lamport1982byzantine,castro1999practical}, which tolerate $f < n/3$ faulty nodes but do not model adversaries that strategically target system structure. An adaptive adversary concentrates on the weakest link~\cite{schneier2000secrets}, suggesting a \emph{reversal}: under random faults, higher $K_{\mathrm{eff}}$ reduces joint failure probability, but under adaptive adversaries, diverse judges may present a wider attack surface.

\begin{proposition}[Weakest-Link Monotonicity; formal statement and proof in Appendix~\ref{app:proof}]
\label{thm:monotonicity}
Replacing any panel member with a pointwise more vulnerable judge can only increase $\mathrm{ASR}^*(\mathcal{P})$, for any adversary including adaptive ones. The stochastic dominance condition holds for 58\% of judge pairs (61/105); non-dominance concentrates among within-tier pairs (72.1\% non-dominant, 31/43) versus cross-tier pairs (21.0\%, 13/62), reflecting that capability-similar judges lack uniform ordering.
\end{proposition}

The 58\% coverage means Proposition~\ref{thm:monotonicity} applies to cross-tier substitutions (where capability gaps are large enough for uniform dominance) but not to within-tier swaps, where judges exhibit comparable vulnerability profiles with crossing points across items. Consequently, the proposition constrains panel design when selecting across capability tiers but does not predict the effect of substitutions within a tier.

The proposition predicts $\beta_2 > 0$ in Equation~\ref{eq:regression}. The independence-based intuition suggests $\beta_1 \leq 0$ under non-adaptive faults; the reversal pattern predicts positive $\beta_1$ for judge-specific attacks and negative for shared-bias attacks. The relative importance of $\eta_{\max}$ versus $K_{\mathrm{eff}}$ depends on $K$: at small $K$, one weak judge flips the majority; at larger $K$, the adversary must compromise multiple judges. We test these predictions across $K \in \{3,5,7\}$ (\S\ref{sec:experiments}).

input.old_string: Per-judge vulnerability under attack $a$ is the fraction of items where judge $j$ is fooled: $\eta_j(a) = \Pr(X_j^a {=} 1)$, estimated empirically over the item set. The weakest-link vulnerability $\eta_{\max}(a) = \max_{j \in \mathcal{P}} \eta_j(a)$ captures the most susceptible member of each panel. The panel attack success rate $\mathrm{ASR}(\mathcal{P}, a)$ is the fraction of items where at least $t$ judges are simultaneously fooled. Panel diversity is quantified by $K_{\mathrm{eff}}$ (Equation~\ref{eq:keff}), computed from pairwise MI between judges' three-category winner labels (model~A wins, model~B wins, tie) on clean data, using the plug-in estimator with Miller--Madow bias correction. The $\exp(-2\,\mathrm{MI}(i,j))$ term measures pairwise alienation: 1 when independent, 0 under full dependence. Under a Gaussian copula this yields $K_{\mathrm{eff}} = K - \frac{1}{K}\sum_{i}\sum_{j \neq i} \rho_{ij}^2$ \citep{nelsen2006copulas}; goodness-of-fit rejects the Gaussian copula for 97--100\% of pairs, yet plug-in MI and closed-form rankings agree closely ($\rho{\approx}0.86$; Appendix~\ref{app:copula_gof}). We also evaluate $\kappa$-diversity ($1 - \bar{\kappa}$, mean pairwise Cohen's $\kappa$; \citealp{kuncheva2003measures}). Together, $\eta_{\max}$ (weakest-link channel) and $K_{\mathrm{eff}}$ (diversity channel) serve as the two predictors in the regression framework below.

Verbosity      & Shared bias & Content padding    & Attention \\

\end{tabular}
\caption{Attack taxonomy. Targeted attacks exploit individual judge weaknesses; shared-bias attacks affect most judges similarly (\S\ref{sec:experiments}).}
\label{tab:attack_taxonomy}
\end{table}

A \emph{panel} $\mathcal{P} = \{J_1, \ldots, J_K\}$ consists of $K$ judges (with $K$ odd) that evaluate a candidate text via majority vote: the text is accepted if at least $t = \lceil K/2 \rceil$ judges approve it. Under an attack $a$, each judge $J_j$ is compromised with marginal failure probability $\eta_j(a) = \Pr(X_j^a = 1)$, where $X_j^a \in \{0,1\}$ denotes the failure indicator. We write $\eta_{\max} = \max_j \eta_j$ for the vulnerability of the weakest judge. The \emph{panel attack success rate} is $\mathrm{ASR}(\mathcal{P}, a) = \Pr\!\bigl(\sum_{j=1}^K X_j^a \geq t\bigr)$.

To quantify diversity, we define the \emph{effective independence} $K_{\mathrm{eff}}$ directly from pairwise mutual information (MI) among judges:
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:keff}
K_{\mathrm{eff}} = \frac{1}{K}\sum_{i=1}^{K} \Bigl[1 + \sum_{j \neq i} \exp\!\bigl(-2 \cdot \mathrm{MI}(i,j)\bigr)\Bigr].
\end{equation}
This formulation computes effective independence from pairwise MI estimates without matrix decomposition, and is more stable for small panels ($K{=}3$). It ranges from $K_{\mathrm{eff}} \approx K$ when judges are nearly independent ($\mathrm{MI} \to 0$) to $K_{\mathrm{eff}} \approx 1$ when judges are highly correlated ($\mathrm{MI} \to \infty$). Motivated by information-theoretic redundancy reduction, one can informally expect joint vulnerability to scale as $\eta_{\mathrm{joint}} \sim K_{\mathrm{eff}} \cdot \eta_{\max}$: independent channels multiply failure probabilities, so fewer effective channels (lower $K_{\mathrm{eff}}$) should reduce panel vulnerability. This motivating relationship assumes non-adaptive faults and independent channels; it serves as intuition rather than a formal bound.

\begin{definition}[Adaptive Adversary]
\label{def:adversary}
A \emph{full-knowledge (oracle) adaptive adversary} has complete knowledge of the panel composition $\mathcal{P}$, the per-judge vulnerability profiles $\{\eta_j(\cdot)\}_{j=1}^K$, and the inter-judge correlation structure. It selects the attack $a^* = \arg\max_{a \in \mathcal{A}} \mathrm{ASR}(\mathcal{P}, a)$ to maximize the panel ASR, yielding $\mathrm{ASR}^*(\mathcal{P}) = \sup_{a \in \mathcal{A}} \mathrm{ASR}(\mathcal{P}, a)$. \end{definition}

This departs from BFT models~\cite{lamport1982byzantine,castro1999practical}, which tolerate $f < n/3$ faulty nodes but do not model adversaries that strategically target system structure. An adaptive adversary concentrates on the weakest link~\cite{schneier2000secrets}, suggesting a \emph{reversal}: under random faults, higher $K_{\mathrm{eff}}$ reduces joint failure probability, but under adaptive adversaries, diverse judges may present a wider attack surface.

\label{thm:monotonicity}
Replacing any panel member with a pointwise more vulnerable judge can only increase $\mathrm{ASR}^*(\mathcal{P})$, for any adversary including adaptive ones. Bottom bars show relative predictive weight.}
7	\label{fig:framework}
8	\end{figure*}
9	
10	Multi-judge panels have become the dominant defense against bias and manipulation in Large Language Model (LLM) evaluation. After \citet{zheng2023judging} demonstrated that individual LLM judges can rival human annotators, subsequent work exposed systematic vulnerabilities: position bias, verbosity preferences, and sycophancy compromise the reliability of any single judge \citep{wang2023fair}. The natural response has been to aggregate decisions across diverse models, an approach inspired by Byzantine fault tolerance (BFT), where majority voting among independent nodes tolerates faulty responses \citep{lamport1982byzantine,castro1999practical}. A recent systematization reports that 7-model committees reduce attack success rates (ASR) from 50--68\% to 10--19\% \citep{almasoud2026security}. Diversity, by this logic, is the key ingredient for secure evaluation, yet this framing conflates two distinct sources of robustness: the quality of individual judges and the independence among them.
11	
12	The conflation matters because the BFT analogy breaks down in the LLM judge setting. BFT adversaries control faulty nodes from within; evaluation adversaries manipulate inputs from without, and shared pretraining corpora create correlated failure modes that violate the independence assumption underlying majority-vote guarantees \citep{schneier2000secrets}. No existing work disentangles diversity from individual robustness across panel sizes, so the relative contribution of each factor to observed ASR reductions remains unclear.
13	
14	We address this gap by decomposing panel vulnerability into two predictors (Figure~\ref{fig:framework}): weakest-link susceptibility ($\eta_{\max}$, the maximum individual attack success rate in a panel) and effective independent channels ($K_{\mathrm{eff}}$, an information-theoretic measure of judge independence). Controlled experiments across 15 models (9 API, 6 local quantized), $K \in \{3,5,7\}$, six attack types, and two multiple-choice benchmarks (Massive Multitask Language Understanding [MMLU] and the AI2 Reasoning Challenge [ARC]) reveal two robust patterns and one metric-sensitive observation.
15	
16	These findings yield three contributions:
17	\begin{enumerate}
18	\item \textbf{Diversity uniformly positively associated with vulnerability.} Both $K_{\mathrm{eff}}$ and $\kappa$-diversity \citep{kuncheva2003measures} confirm a positive association with panel attack success in all 12 conditions (12/12 direction under OLS and generalized additive model bootstrap). However, the diversity--capability confound ($r{=}0.70$--$0.81$) precludes causal interpretation: Cinelli--Hazlett robustness values do not exceed the confound in 69\% of conditions (\S\ref{sec:dominance}, \S\ref{sec:gam_taxonomy}).
19	\item \textbf{Diminishing weakest link.} $\eta_{\max}$'s predictive power declines monotonically with panel size: meta-analytic pooled $\hat{\beta}_{\mathrm{std}}$ falls from $0.264$ [$0.158, 0.369$] at $K{=}3$ to $0.102$ [$-0.055, 0.259$] at $K{=}5$ to $0.084$ [$-0.083, 0.251$] at $K{=}7$; the confidence interval crosses zero at $K{\geq}5$. The diversity significance trajectory, however, depends on the metric: $K_{\mathrm{eff}}$ significance increases ($4 \to 7 \to 8$/12) while $\kappa$-diversity decreases ($8 \to 7 \to 6$/12), indicating that the $K$-dependent pattern is operationalization-sensitive (\S\ref{sec:cross_k}).
20	\item \textbf{Aggregation as predictability control.} Aggregation rules modulate how much variance panel composition explains ($R^2$: threshold 0.83, Bayesian 0.09). Bayesian calibration attenuates $K_{\mathrm{eff}}$ (5+/1$-$) but $\eta_{\max}$ persists (9/12), so the defense is partial (\S\ref{sec:aggregation}, \S\ref{sec:analysis}).
21	\end{enumerate}

23	All findings are associational; the diversity--capability confound ($r{=}0.70$--$0.81$; \S\ref{sec:analysis}) precludes causal claims.

\section{Threat Model and Problem Formulation}
\label{sec:threat_model}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{llll}
\toprule
\textbf{Attack} & \textbf{Category} & \textbf{Mechanism} & \textbf{Target} \\
\midrule
Prompt inj.    & Targeted    & Override instruct. & Decision \\
Score manip.   & Targeted    & Numeric anchoring  & Score \\
Sycophancy     & Shared bias & Flattery/agreement & Preference \\
Verbosity      & Shared bias & Content padding    & Attention \\
Position bias  & Shared bias & Response reorder   & Position \\
Authority bias & Shared bias & Credential appeal  & Trust \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Attack taxonomy. Targeted attacks exploit individual judge weaknesses; shared-bias attacks affect most judges similarly (\S\ref{sec:experiments}).}
\label{tab:attack_taxonomy}
\end{table}

A \emph{panel} $\mathcal{P} = \{J_1, \ldots, J_K\}$ consists of $K$ judges (with $K$ odd) that evaluate a candidate text via majority vote: the text is accepted if at least $t = \lceil K/2 \rceil$ judges approve it. Under an attack $a$, each judge $J_j$ is compromised with marginal failure probability $\eta_j(a) = \Pr(X_j^a = 1)$, where $X_j^a \in \{0,1\}$ denotes the failure indicator. We write $\eta_{\max} = \max_j \eta_j$ for the vulnerability of the weakest judge. The \emph{panel attack success rate} is $\mathrm{ASR}(\mathcal{P}, a) = \Pr\!\bigl(\sum_{j=1}^K X_j^a \geq t\bigr)$.

To quantify diversity, we define the \emph{effective independence} $K_{\mathrm{eff}}$ directly from pairwise mutual information (MI) among judges:
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:keff}
K_{\mathrm{eff}} = \frac{1}{K}\sum_{i=1}^{K} \Bigl[1 + \sum_{j \neq i} \exp\!\bigl(-2 \cdot \mathrm{MI}(i,j)\bigr)\Bigr].
\end{equation}
This formulation computes effective independence from pairwise MI estimates without matrix decomposition, and is more stable for small panels ($K{=}3$). It ranges from $K_{\mathrm{eff}} \approx K$ when judges are nearly independent ($\mathrm{MI} \to 0$) to $K_{\mathrm{eff}} \approx 1$ when judges are highly correlated ($\mathrm{MI} \to \infty$). Motivated by information-theoretic redundancy reduction, one can informally expect joint vulnerability to scale as $\eta_{\mathrm{joint}} \sim K_{\mathrm{eff}} \cdot \eta_{\max}$: independent channels multiply failure probabilities, so fewer effective channels (lower $K_{\mathrm{eff}}$) should reduce panel vulnerability. This motivating relationship assumes non-adaptive faults and independent channels; it serves as intuition rather than a formal bound.

\begin{definition}[Adaptive Adversary]
\label{def:adversary}
A \emph{full-knowledge (oracle) adaptive adversary} has complete knowledge of the panel composition $\mathcal{P}$, the per-judge vulnerability profiles $\{\eta_j(\cdot)\}_{j=1}^K$, and the inter-judge correlation structure. It selects the attack $a^* = \arg\max_{a \in \mathcal{A}} \mathrm{ASR}(\mathcal{P}, a)$ to maximize the panel ASR, yielding $\mathrm{ASR}^*(\mathcal{P}) = \sup_{a \in \mathcal{A}} \mathrm{ASR}(\mathcal{P}, a)$. This oracle model represents an \emph{upper bound} on adversarial capability; realistic adversaries with partial knowledge of panel composition would achieve lower ASR.
\end{definition}

This departs from BFT models~\cite{lamport1982byzantine,castro1999practical}, which tolerate $f < n/3$ faulty nodes but do not model adversaries that strategically target system structure. An adaptive adversary concentrates on the weakest link~\cite{schneier2000secrets}, suggesting a \emph{reversal}: under random faults, higher $K_{\mathrm{eff}}$ reduces joint failure probability, but under adaptive adversaries, diverse judges may present a wider attack surface.

\begin{proposition}[Weakest-Link Monotonicity; formal statement and proof in Appendix~\ref{app:proof}]
\label{thm:monotonicity}
Replacing any panel member with a pointwise more vulnerable judge can only increase $\mathrm{ASR}^*(\mathcal{P})$, for any adversary including adaptive ones. The stochastic dominance condition holds for 58\% of judge pairs (61/105); non-dominance concentrates among within-tier pairs (72.1\% non-dominant, 31/43) versus cross-tier pairs (21.0\%, 13/62), reflecting that capability-similar judges lack uniform ordering.
\end{proposition}

The proposition predicts $\beta_2 > 0$ in Equation~\ref{eq:regression}; the reversal pattern predicts positive $\beta_1$ under adversarial conditions. The relative importance of $\eta_{\max}$ versus $K_{\mathrm{eff}}$ depends on $K$: at small $K$, one weak judge flips the majority; at larger $K$, the adversary must compromise multiple judges (\S\ref{sec:experiments}).
